title: Profiling tooling and scripts - perf CI jobs, flamegraphs, trace collectors, runbook
content:
Purpose:
This working doc collects the profiling tooling, scripts, and CI jobs we use to detect and investigate serving runtime performance regressions. It is intended for engineers on eng-serving-runtime and SREs who need quick diagnostics and reproducible artifacts (flamegraphs, traces, perf reports) when latency/throughput changes are observed.

Scope:
- Perf CI jobs that run on PRs and nightly benchmarks
- Local and cluster trace collectors (OTel, Jaeger, eBPF helpers)
- Flamegraph generation for CPU and GPU stack traces
- Runbook steps for triage of latency regressions / throughput drops
- Storage, retention, and naming conventions for artifacts

Quick TL;DR (for on-call / triage):
1) Reproduce under load in perf staging: run ./tools/load-test/run.sh --config=ci/p95-config.json
2) Capture a 60s CPU+syscall profile: ./tools/prof/collect_cpu_perf.sh --pid <pid> --duration 60 --out /tmp/profile1.data
3) Generate flamegraph: ./tools/prof/make_flamegraph.sh /tmp/profile1.data > /tmp/flame.svg
4) If GPU: run nvprof/nvtx capture + collectmetrics (see GPU section)
5) Upload artifacts to perf-bucket/redwood-perf/<job>-<date> and create JIRA with links

Perf CI jobs (what we run and why):
- pr/perf-smoke (on PR): lightweight 30s single-instance run that measures p50/p95/p99 for a small prompt set. Triggers: PR to serving-runtime core, changes to batching/cache code.
- nightly/perf-bench (nightly): 10-minute multi-client run against perf staging. Produces: latency histograms, flamegraphs, memory profiles, kv-cache hit rates. Baseline auto-comparison (see ci/compare_benchmarks.py).
- weekly/gpu-regression (weekly): runs representative GPU models (gpt-like medium/large) with capture of GPU metrics and NVTX segments.

CI job implementation notes:
- Jobs run on our perf Kubernetes cluster. They spin up a dedicated inference node pool with pinned instance types for determinism.
- Use k8s annotations to label pods with perf-run=<job-id> for easy selection when collecting traces.
- Jobs write artifacts to s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/<job>/<date>/<commit>/, plus a symlink latest/ for dashboards.
- Bench harness: tools/load-test/bench_runner.py (python) — accepts concurrency, qps, and seq_len distribution configs.
- Compare script: ci/compare_benchmarks.py produces delta table and basic significance check (bootstrap p95 diffs).

Local profiling tooling (scripts we use frequently):
- tools/prof/collect_cpu_perf.sh (wrapper around linux perf): collects perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -o out.data for duration. Includes sudo instructions and a helper to translate to folded stacks via perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl
- tools/prof/make_flamegraph.sh: runs flamegraph.pl on folded stacks and emits flame.svg
- tools/prof/collect_pyspy.sh: uses py-spy to capture Python-level flamegraphs for Python worker processes (safe in prod if sampling-only).
- tools/prof/collect_eBPF.sh: uses bpftrace scripts to summarize syscalls, wakeups, and scheduler events. Useful to detect IO waits or excessive context switches.
- tools/prof/collect_gpu_nvtx.sh: injects NVTX ranges via runtime hooks and uses ncu or nvprof to capture timeline. Also collects nvidia-smi pmon logs for utilization samples.
- tools/prof/collect_heap.sh: for native heap (jemalloc) we run jeprof dumps and translate to flamegraphs with jeprof-to-flame. For Python we use tracemalloc snapshots.

Trace collectors & distributed traces:
- We use OpenTelemetry SDKs instrumented in the serving runtime. Sampling: default 1% in prod, override to 100% for perf CI jobs via OTEL_SAMPLER=always_on.
- Collector: otel-collector deployment in perf cluster routes to Jaeger and to s3 (via otel-exporter) for artifact storage.
- When investigating tail latency, enable 100% traces for the offending route for a short window and collect spans + raw payloads (sanitized).
- Jaeger UI queries: service=serving-runtime, operation=GenerateTokens or SendBatchRequest. Use duration>100ms filter for p99 explorations.

Flamegraphs (best practices):
- Always record both kernel+user stacks (perf record -g -a --call-graph dwarf). Kernel context often explains futex/waiting hotspots.
- Produce annotated flamegraphs with colormap: resolving sources (python C-extension, nvml drivers, runtime.c) and link to source files using addr2line when possible.
- Keep SVGs under 5MB; for large traces use sampling downsample script: tools/prof/downsample_flame.py
- Naming convention: <job>-<service>-<commit>-<type>-<timestamp>.svg (e.g., nightly-serving-abc123-cpu-20250219T2130.svg)

GPU profiling specifics:
- Add NVTX regions in critical code paths: attention, matmul, layernorm, quant/dequant. We prefer scoped RAII macros in C++ and context managers in Python.
- Use ncu (Nsight Compute) for kernel-level metrics and nvprof/Nsight Systems for timeline traces. Capture both SM utilization and memory bandwidth.
- Common regressions exposed: increased kernel launch overhead, degraded occupancy due to changed shapes, extra memcpy synchronization.

Data we capture per run (artifact list):
- latency_hist.json (p50/p90/p95/p99, raw latency samples)
- flame_cpu.svg (user+kernel)
- flame_python.svg (py-spy)
- perf_record.data (raw perf record)
- jaeger_trace_ids.txt (list of 50 slow trace ids)
- gpu_nsys.qdrep or ncu_report.json
- mem_profile.txt or heap_profile.prof
- bench_metadata.json (commit, image tag, node types, input distribution)

Runbook: Triage steps for a p95/p99 regression (concise):
1) Validate the regression: compare nightly baseline (last known good) vs current. Use ci/compare_benchmarks.py. If delta < 5% on p95, consider noise.
2) Check recent commits between baseline and current: git log --oneline <baseline>..HEAD in serving-runtime and related repos. Look for batching, kernel, or RPC changes.
3) Re-run perf CI with traces enabled (nightly/perf-bench with OTEL_SAMPLER=always_on and collect_cpu_perf.sh).
4) Obtain flamegraphs for both baseline and regression; diff visually and with tools/prof/flame_diff.py to highlight stack growth.
5) If CPU stacks show futex/wait/wakeup, run eBPF collector to inspect scheduling wakes.
6) If kernel/syscall hotspots, correlate with syscalls list (tools/prof/syscall_summary.txt) and check network IO.
7) If GPU slowdown suspected: collect nsys timeline, check for memcpy or kernel queuing delays, verify cudnn/cuda version changes.
8) Narrow to specific model layer: use instrumented NVTX ranges or fine-grained span names to find which layer increased time.
9) Patch candidate fix in small PR and run pr/perf-smoke to verify no regressions.
10) Rollout plan: canary -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with metric alerts for p95 and error rates. Use automatic fallback to previous model variant if latency exceeds SLA.

Alerting & thresholds:
- p95 increase > 25% relative to baseline -> create incident.
- absolute p99 > configured SLA for route -> page on-call and trigger perf job.
- memory growth > 100MB per hour -> automatic heap dump and retention.

Artifact retention and storage:
- Perf artifacts stored in s3 bucket for 180 days. Large GPU nsight files moved to cold-storage after 14 days.
- Naming and tagging for easy query via S3: tags: service=serving-runtime, job=<job>, commit=<commit>. Use lifecycle policies to expire.

Common scripts (path + short usage):
- tools/prof/collect_cpu_perf.sh --pid <pid> --duration 60 --out /tmp/out.data
- tools/prof/make_flamegraph.sh /tmp/out.data > /tmp/flame.svg
- tools/prof/collect_pyspy.sh --pid <pid> --duration 45 --format svg --out py_flame.svg
- tools/prof/collect_eBPF.sh --duration 30 --out ebpf-summary.txt
- tools/load-test/run.sh --config ci/p95-config.json --out artifacts/ --concurrency 64
- ci/compare_benchmarks.py artifacts/baseline.json artifacts/current.json --report out.html

Unresolved questions / TODOs (working list):
- Automate side-by-side flame diffs in the perf dashboard (assigned: Avery).
- Add GPU kernel-level attribution into flamegraph view (investigate tools or custom exporter).
- Improve sampling strategy for production to capture more p99 traces without high overhead. Consider adaptive sampling triggered by latency spikes.
- Document safe py-spy usage in production and security review for sampling.

Notes / context (why these choices):
- We prioritize low-overhead sampling in prod; CI and perf staging prioritize completeness.
- Flamegraphs are the team lingua franca for hotspots; keep generation reproducible from raw perf records.
- Instrumentation (OTel spans, NVTX) should be lightweight and gated by env flags to avoid overhead during normal traffic.

References and example commands (copy-paste friendly):
- Generate folded stacks from perf: sudo perf script -i perf.data | ./tools/prof/stackcollapse-perf.pl > folded.stacks
- Make svg: ./tools/prof/flamegraph.pl folded.stacks > flame.svg
- py-spy (record): sudo py-spy record -o py_flame.svg --format svg --pid <pid> --duration 30
- nsight systems capture (container): nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_report --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --duration=30 --target-pid <pid>

Contact / owners:
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime (oncall) -> #eng-serving-runtime Slack
- Tooling owners: Maya Patel (profiling scripts), Avery Chen (perf dashboard)

Revision history:
- 2024-05-10 initial draft (Maya)
- 2024-07-02 added GPU NVTX guidance (Avery)
- 2025-02-20 updated retention policy and CI job names (Maya)

End of doc.
